item.title: Meta is betting the house on AI — CFO warns the stakes are 'really bad' if it flops
item.author: Yahoo Finance
item.description:
Meta is betting the house on AI — CFO warns the stakes are 'really bad' if it flops
2026-10-13
Por Yahoo Finance
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/meta-is-betting-the-house-on-ai--cfo-warns-the-stakes-are-really-bad-if-it-flops-133413709.html
Oh, to be Meta's (META) very well-regarded CFO, Susan Li right now.
Li — who has worked at Meta for 18 years, mostly in financial roles — is the person tasked with overseeing the company's financial statements and ensuring Meta invests in projects with the highest potential return for investors. It's also her job to assess risk and push back against the growth-at-all-costs duo of Mark Zuckerberg and Alexandr Wang.
Right now, the job sure seems like a more Herculean task compared to years past.
Wang revealed in a new episode of Stripe (STRI.PVT) co-founder John Collison's Cheeky Pints podcast that Li pulled him aside "many times" during an executive offsite in Hawaii to warn that if the company's newest model didn't work, it would be bad news financially.
"And I think this is, and I kind of viscerally remember this. We were in Hawaii at the end of last year. It was kind of like the whole exec team got together," Wang said. "And yeah, Susan pulled me aside many times and was like, you know, I just want to tell you if this doesn't work, this is going to be really, really bad. It's going to be very, very bad in financial terms. It's like, it has to be good. If it's good, it's all good. We're great. But if it's bad, it's really, really, really bad."
Meta's new model appears to work quite well. Now people just need to pay for it to justify the gargantuan investment Li signed off on.
The company officially debuted its next-generation frontier AI models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, this week from its Meta Superintelligence Labs.
These frontier models represent a dramatic surge in intelligence by featuring deep multistep reasoning, dynamic memory retention, and native multitool execution capabilities across web and desktop environments.
"Yesterday's launch of Muse Wonder and Wonder Full is Meta's first frontier-class release and, in our view, is at or near parity with leading frontier labs," said Pivotal Research analyst Jeff Wlodarczak. "On Meta's benchmark set Wonder Full leads on roughly 7 of 14 tests in Meta's benchmark set (including internal ones), with strong results on long horizon coding, legal agents, and memory, while scoring second on the independent Artificial Analysis Index (56 vs 58 for Claude Opus 5.5. Wonder is priced at $4/$20 per million tokens, matching Opus 5.5, while the stronger Wonder Full is sold only through Muse Code subscriptions ($50-$200 a month) rather than the API, which supports our view that Meta will monetize through paid tiers and enterprise rather than open weights."

item.title: Netflix could stop its stock free-fall with these 4 actions: KeyBanc analyst
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Netflix could stop its stock free-fall with these 4 actions: KeyBanc analyst
2026-10-13
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/netflix-could-stop-its-stock-free-fall-with-these-4-actions-keybanc-analyst-130507914.html
Netflix (NFLX) won't be spending the rest of 2026 integrating its once-sought-after prize in Warner Bros. Discovery. That pure joy goes to the well-paid exec team cobbled together by Skydance (SKYD) media titan David Ellison.
But what the streaming pioneer should do, Wall Street says, is articulate a plan on its Oct. 20 earnings call to arrest the stock's crash. Shares are down 25% this year and have steadily declined since mid-April.
KeyBanc analyst Justin Patterson said in a note on Tuesday that he would like to hear four actions from Netflix management next week.
We don't think Patterson is alone in hoping for clarity on these fronts:
- "The first action is content investment. We are already seeing this in areas like live events (which represents ~5% of content spend, and will continue to be measured) and licensed (which underperformed in 2H25 and has had improved content coming in over the course of 2026). As the content quality improves, we believe this could support both pricing power and ads monetization."
- "The second action is product. Again, this has been occurring over the past year through areas like the new home screen and AI recommendation models. The new home screen is particularly interesting as it promoted live events and gaming more at the start, which we believe had some negative impact on engagement (i.e., recommendation algorithms were less optimized here than for series and films). As Netflix has learned more about how to promote this content, we believe this headwind is fading. We also believe there is more potential for TF1 type deals. Over a longer time horizon, we believe both gaming and potentially another ad tier could become more meaningful levers."
- "The third action is operating expense reductions. Puck recently wrote an article about Netflix planning a roughly 5% workforce reduction, which would correspond to 800-850 employees. From 2019-2025, Netflix's headcount has increased from ~8,600 to ~16,000. Given the size of the company today and potential savings from AI, we suspect there is room for some degree of expense realignment."
- "Finally, we believe it could make sense to explore a dividend. Most media and entertainment stocks have paid dividends, and we have observed more large-cap internet companies doing the same to broaden the shareholder base (e.g., Alphabet, Meta (META). While this would not change the growth discussion, we do believe it could improve investor sentiment, support the P/E multiple, and potentially lessen the focus on large M&A."

item.title: Nvidia, AMD, Google, and Meta team up on global blueprint for data center design
item.author: Daniel Howley
item.description:
Nvidia, AMD, Google, and Meta team up on global blueprint for data center design
2026-10-13
Por Daniel Howley
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/nvidia-amd-google-and-meta-team-up-on-global-blueprint-for-data-center-design-150000023.html
Nvidia (NVDA) is joining rival AMD (AMD) along with partners Google (GOOG, GOOGL) and Meta (META) to establish a new open specification for data center design.
Called the Open Data Center Specification v0.7, the standard serves as a blueprint for building data centers, covering everything from the physical layout of the buildings to cooling and power architecture.
The chip giant also said it's teaming with Google, Meta, and Microsoft (MSFT) to create the OCP Grid Resilience Specification, which serves as a standard for how data centers respond to power disruptions, ensuring they can rapidly return to full operation.
According to Nvidia, the two specifications provide everyone from system makers to colocation providers and data center operators with a set of predefined templates for building data centers without having to contend with a slew of different customer designs.
Data centers are incredibly complex facilities that require large amounts of power and cooling to keep the chips inside from overheating and failing. And adding custom designs and quirks can slow construction timelines.
Open standards could change that, allowing builders to bring new data centers online faster. And the faster data centers go up, the more chips, systems, and networking components Nvidia can sell.
At the same time, data centers are facing increasing pushback from communities across the US, with some towns and counties imposing moratoriums or outright bans to stop companies from building them.
New York has enacted a statewide, one-year moratorium on data center construction, and Texas has halted new projects until it can determine the impact that connecting more power-hungry sites will have on its electrical grid.
President Trump has pushed back against any resistance to data centers, saying they'll be moneymakers for states.
Read the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance.

item.title: Intel aims to boost AI turnaround with new GPU chips to take on Nvidia
item.author: Daniel Howley
item.description:
Intel aims to boost AI turnaround with new GPU chips to take on Nvidia
2026-10-13
Por Daniel Howley
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/intel-aims-to-boost-ai-turnaround-with-new-gpu-chips-to-take-on-nvidia-192916083.html
Intel's (INTC) turnaround effort is getting a strong boost from the global AI build-out, which is driving increased demand for its central processing units (CPUs).
But the company is also expanding further into the graphics processing unit (GPU) market with the debut of its Intel GPU D-Series processors. Formerly codenamed Crescent Island, the D-Series chips are designed for AI inferencing, running AI models and services.
Rather than individual chips that slot into server blades like Nvidia's (NVDA) Blackwell processors, Intel's D-Series GPUs are deployed via PCIe cards, similar in appearance to the graphics cards gamers install in desktop computers.
Intel said it's working with a number of OEMs, ODMs, neoclouds, and others to roll out D-Series systems, including ASUS (2357.TW), HPE (HPE), Dell (DELL), Supermicro, and others.
Intel has been working to gain a greater foothold in the GPU market, ranging from consumer products to the data center, including its Gaudi AI accelerator and GPU Flex Series cards.
Intel stock is up 183% year to date and roughly 175% over the past 12 months, largely driven by interest in its CPUs.
The processors, which fell out of favor in the early days of the generative AI explosion, have become increasingly important for AI providers and data center builders with the advent of AI agents.
That's because while GPUs and AI accelerators power the AI models and agents that rely on them, the tasks agents perform, such as sorting through databases, launching apps, loading websites, and more, run on CPUs.
But Intel is facing increasing competition in the CPU data center race from longtime rival AMD (AMD), which is rapidly growing its share of data center revenue in the space.
Arm-based (ARM) CPUs are also gaining a greater foothold in the data center, thanks to Nvidia's decision to launch standalone CPU racks running its Grace chip.
Qualcomm (QCOM) has also entered the fight with its own Arm-based CPUs, AI accelerators, memory products, and networking capabilities as it seeks to diversify beyond its reliance on the smartphone market.
Read the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance.

item.title: Hall, Woodford win Nobel prize for work on how to stabilise economies
item.author: Simon Johnson; Johan Ahlander
item.description:
Hall, Woodford win Nobel prize for work on how to stabilise economies
2026-10-13
Por Simon Johnson; Johan Ahlander
https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/americans-hall-woodford-win-2026-095604833.html
Hall, Woodford win Nobel prize for work on how to stabilise economies
By Simon Johnson and Johan Ahlander
STOCKHOLM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize on Monday for decades of work developing ground-up models currently used by central banks and finance ministries across the world to stabilise economies.
"With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.
Woodford and Hall are frequently name-checked by the world's top central banks which, after a 2022 inflation surge in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, are currently grappling with the energy shock triggered by the Iran war.
One of the laureates' key insights is that economies could only be kept on an even keel by taking into account the millions of decisions made at a micro-level by households and businesses, rather than by using top-down theories of how economies work.
"Authorities shouldn't view stabilization of the economy as an exercise that is simply conducted by people pulling levers to control the economy independently of what people in the economy understand about this," Columbia University's Woodford, 70, told a news conference.
In contrast to the oil shocks of the 1970s, when central banks struggled to combat sky-high inflation, Woodford said the new framework was useful during the global financial crisis of the late-2000s to bolster traditional tools of monetary policy.
"Making more explicit statements about the likely future path of interest rate policy, as opposed to relying on simply being able to cut interest rates further immediately, that was an important part of the policy response in the years from 2009 onward," he said.
Beyond so-called "forward guidance" on the future path of monetary policy, the work of Woodford - and Hall, 83, at Stanford University – promoted other concepts used today such as the idea of "sticky" inflation when price changes lag changes in demand.

Hall, Woodford win Nobel prize for work on how to stabilise economies

Por Simon Johnson; Johan Ahlander

https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/americans-hall-woodford-win-2026-095604833.html

Hall, Woodford win Nobel prize for work on how to stabilise economies

By Simon Johnson and Johan Ahlander

STOCKHOLM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize on Monday for decades of work developing ground-up models currently used by central banks and finance ministries across the world to stabilise economies.

"With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.

Woodford and Hall are frequently name-checked by the world's top central banks which, after a 2022 inflation surge in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, are currently grappling with the energy shock triggered by the Iran war.

One of the laureates' key insights is that economies could only be kept on an even keel by taking into account the millions of decisions made at a micro-level by households and businesses, rather than by using top-down theories of how economies work.

"Authorities shouldn't view stabilization of the economy as an exercise that is simply conducted by people pulling levers to control the economy independently of what people in the economy understand about this," Columbia University's Woodford, 70, told a news conference.

In contrast to the oil shocks of the 1970s, when central banks struggled to combat sky-high inflation, Woodford said the new framework was useful during the global financial crisis of the late-2000s to bolster traditional tools of monetary policy.

"Making more explicit statements about the likely future path of interest rate policy, as opposed to relying on simply being able to cut interest rates further immediately, that was an important part of the policy response in the years from 2009 onward," he said.

Beyond so-called "forward guidance" on the future path of monetary policy, the work of Woodford - and Hall, 83, at Stanford University – promoted other concepts used today such as the idea of "sticky" inflation when price changes lag changes in demand.

Another is the "output gap", a measure of demand pressure building up in an economy and how efficiently resources are being used, with the goal of stabilisation policy being to steer that gap towards zero.

CORE CENTRAL BANK CONCEPTS

Hall has served as adviser to the US Treasury Department, the Justice Department and the Federal Reserve Board.

His insight in a 1978 paper that household decisions on consumption are a perfect indicator of their expectations was used by Woodford in a model on how consumption is determined.

Hall called the prize "a wonderful surprise" in a statement.

"I've spent my career trying to understand how the economy works," he said. "When I thought I had a new idea, the next step was to find out whether it was actually new, whether it was right, and whether it mattered."

Woodford also showed that central banks can stimulate or suppress economic activity by adjusting interest rates, rather than just by the amount of money in circulation.

Such concepts remain core to central banking today. Forward guidance became especially important after the 2008 financial crisis, when rates were near zero or even negative and standard monetary policy seemed to be out of ammunition.

Now, however, some are questioning how relevant it is given the amount of uncertainty in the global economy – with new US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh a notable sceptic.

The economics prize, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is the final award to be given out this year and is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).

item.title: Micron, SK Hynix stocks fall as Chinese memory maker announces progress in new design
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
Micron, SK Hynix stocks fall as Chinese memory maker announces progress in new design
2026-10-13
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/micron-sk-hynix-stocks-fall-as-chinese-memory-maker-announces-progress-in-new-design-123824149.html
What happened: Micron (MU) and SK Hynix (000660.KS, SKHY) stocks fell 3% as Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) tumbled 4% alongside the broader South Korean stock market.
What's behind the move: The move comes after Chinese memory maker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) (688825.SS) announced significant progress in a new memory-cell design aimed at increasing storage density, an area of innovation also being pursued by the largest memory makers in the world, including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron.
CXMT aims to introduce a new server memory product built on the architecture by the end of 2026, company president Cao Kanyu said at an industry event in Shanghai over the weekend.
What else do you need to know? Micron stock is down roughly 16% from its all-time high in June.
The company posted strong quarterly results in September.
Last week, D.A. Davidson's Gil Luria lifted his price target for the memory chip manufacturer to $3,000, the highest on Wall Street, citing long-term growth opportunities tied to artificial intelligence.
The revised target marks a big jump from the firm's previous $2,100 estimate.
Ines Ferre is a senior business reporter for Yahoo Finance.

item.title: 'AI 3.0 is the interface': Salesforce stock pops on BoA upgrade
item.author: Michael B Kelley
item.description:
'AI 3.0 is the interface': Salesforce stock pops on BoA upgrade
2026-10-13
Por Michael B Kelley
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/ai-30-is-the-interface-salesforce-stock-pops-on-boa-upgrade-141148660.html
Salesforce stock (CRM) rose as much as 5% Monday morning after Bank of America upgraded it to Buy from Underperform after deciding that previous worries that AI would cut Salesforce out of enterprise software were overdone.
BofA analyst Tal Liani raised his price target to $285 from $160, a 78% increase. The new target sits about 24% above Friday's close of $229.13. The stock was up about 2% shortly before 10 a.m. ET.
"If AI 1.0 was the model, AI 2.0 was the agent, then AI 3.0 is the interface," Liani wrote in a note to clients Monday.
That shift was the risk BofA had flagged earlier: As workers hand tasks to AI assistants, they may stop opening Salesforce apps at all. That fear hammered many software stocks for a stretch, though the group has rallied sharply since the end of June, with Salesforce among the top performers.
Conversations with chief information officers and other market participants changed BofA's call. Large companies, the note said, are unlikely to replace the platforms that house their business logic, data, workflows, and compliance frameworks.
"If anything, AI should deepen dependence on these platforms," Liani wrote.
BofA argued that Salesforce covers all four layers a company needs to put AI to work: data (Informatica and Data 360), applications (Sales Cloud and Service Cloud), agents (Agentforce), and the interface (Slack, Claudeforce).
The "SaaSpocalypse" narrative, the firm added, "overstates the extent to which losing the user interface translates into losing platform value for Salesforce."
Read more: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff: 'We cannot let AI become social media 2.0'
BofA also sees early signs that growth will pick up, including strong growth in net new annual order value, a bookings measure, and faster gains at Slack. It raised its forecasts for subscription and support revenue growth in fiscal 2028 and 2029 to 10.4% and 10.5%, respectively, from 9.9% and 10.2%.
The main near-term risk, according to the note, is that companies adopt AI more slowly than expected, since Salesforce's AI revenue is still small.

item.title: Gas prices on track to break record for most days above $4 a gallon: Chart of the Day
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
Gas prices on track to break record for most days above $4 a gallon: Chart of the Day
2026-10-13
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/gas-prices-on-track-to-break-record-for-most-days-above-4-a-gallon-chart-of-the-day-172053108.html
Gasoline prices have eased in recent weeks, but the national average is still on track to break the record for the most days above $4 per gallon in a single year.
The national average for regular gasoline stood at $4.35 a gallon on Monday, about $0.04 less than a month ago, but about $1.27 more than a year ago, according to AAA data.
By Wednesday, prices are expected to set the 2022 record for the total number of days in a year spent above $4 per gallon, according to Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy.
Even though gasoline prices have come off their peak of north of $4.50 in May, they remain at record highs for this time of year, JPMorgan analysts noted last month.
Meanwhile, the national average for diesel stood at $6.25 per gallon on Monday, about $0.10 less than a month ago. Diesel costs directly affect the prices of goods and services, given how heavily it is relied upon for farming, trucking, and deliveries.
Because refineries produce diesel and heating oil from the same supply, approaching winter demand is expected to keep upward pressure on prices.
Gasoline and heating oil futures, which move in lockstep with diesel, show a year-to-date surge of more than 86% and 124%, respectively, according to AlphaSpace data.
Oil prices rose on Monday in the wake of deadly Middle East attacks and amid growing doubts over a Russia-Ukraine "energy ceasefire" announced by President Trump over the weekend.
Brent crude (BZ=F) rose to $106 per barrel, while West Texas Intermediate crude (CL=F) dropped to $93 a barrel.
Meanwhile, crews were still assessing the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias, which prompted two major refinery shutdowns along the Gulf Coast.
Ines Ferre is a Senior Business Reporter for Yahoo Finance covering the US stock market, publicly traded companies, and commodities.

item.title: 3 charts sum up why many US households are struggling right now
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
3 charts sum up why many US households are struggling right now
2026-10-13
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/article/3-charts-sum-up-why-many-us-households-are-struggling-right-now-153911897.html
The S&P 500 (^GSPC) trading near a record high doesn't mean all is fine and dandy in the US economy. Quite the contrary for many households as they battle higher costs for gas, fuel, and medical insurance this year.
Consumer sentiment fell to 46.3 in October, down 1.8 points from September's reading of 48.1, according to the latest from the University of Michigan. The result represented a five-month low.
Pressured household finances have appeared in the crop of third quarter earnings reports from packaged food companies. Food and beverage giant PepsiCo (PEP) slashed its full-year profit outlook last week. That came on the heels of spice-maker McCormick (MKC) reporting sluggish demand in its most recent quarter.
"We don't expect the consumer to suddenly become in a much better place in the next 12 to 18 months," PepsiCo CEO Ramon Laguarta said on the company's earnings call.
Here are several charts from the Goldman Sachs team that shed light on the realities facing many US households, and why a lot of consumer companies are struggling.
Household debt is on the rise
With the cost of living remaining high, households are taking on more debt to get by. Household debt now tops $18 trillion.
Personal savings are dwindling
In addition to taking on more debt, households have dipped into their savings to spend on what they need to spend on. Personal savings rates are below the long-term average.
Read more: How to protect your savings against inflation
Stagnant wages
Inflation has eaten up worker wages. In September, average hourly earnings rose just 0.1% month over month and 3% year over year, according to Labor Department data. Government data found that, in August, inflation increased 3.4% year over year.

item.title: US mortgage bond funds suffer one of worst outflows since 2021
item.author: Zahra Tayeb
item.description:
US mortgage bond funds suffer one of worst outflows since 2021
2026-10-13
Por Zahra Tayeb
https://finance.yahoo.com/real-estate/articles/us-mortgage-bond-funds-suffer-142622735.html
(Bloomberg) -- Investors fled US mortgage bond funds at historic levels over the past three weeks, with outflows ranking among the seven worst since the start of 2021, as surging interest rates spur a flight from volatility.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The Bloomberg US Mortgage Backed Securities Index marked its second worst performance on record in September. The selling follows a spike in Treasury yields to multi-decade highs, fueled by surging oil prices, inflation concerns, and expectations of Federal Reserve interest rate hikes.
Mortgage-backed securities are highly sensitive to sudden fluctuations in bond yields, which serve as the benchmarks for borrowing costs throughout the economy. When interest rates rise, homeowners tend to stop refinancing their home loans, keeping investors locked into lower-yielding securities for longer than they may had previously expected.
"Fed policy tightening and a flatter curve may reduce demand from banks, a key source of MBS demand," Erica Adelberg, senior MBS strategist at Bloomberg Intelligence, wrote. "On the positive side, MBS supply should trend lower into year-end, with the highest mortgage rates since 2023 reducing refinancing and home-purchase demand and potentially slowing home-price and loan-size appreciation."
The Treasuries selloff in September sent yields on long-dated bonds to 24-year highs. Coupled with the underperformance in mortgage-backed securities on an excess return basis, the MBS index logged the second-most negative year-to-date total return in its 50-year history, Adelberg said.
Most Read from Bloomberg Businessweek
2026 Bloomberg L.P.

item.title: In 17 US cities, new homes are now cheaper than old ones
item.author: Claire Boston
item.description:
In 17 US cities, new homes are now cheaper than old ones
2026-10-13
Por Claire Boston
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/in-17-us-cities-new-homes-are-now-cheaper-than-old-ones-165413642.html
Historically, buying a new-construction home meant paying a premium over older options. But that's starting to reverse as builders deal with rising inventory and an ongoing sales slump.
In some places where building activity has been most aggressive, like the Sun Belt, new homes now sell for less on a price-per-square-foot basis than existing homes, according to Zillow data. In Austin, new construction homes now carry a 19.3% discount to existing homes, while in Raleigh, they're 14.2% cheaper.
Read more: Is 8% next? Why mortgage rates have surged, and may stay higher for longer
Homebuilders have been cutting prices and offering incentives such as closing-cost assistance and mortgage rate buydowns to lure buyers. As of August, builders' months of supply — an industry measure of how long it would take to sell off all inventory at today's sales pace — sits at 8.5. More than six months of supply indicates a market where buyers have the upper hand.
Building has been uneven across the country, and in places where new construction is rare, such as the Northeast and the Midwest, buying a new home still usually comes at a hefty premium over existing options.
Claire Boston is a senior reporter for Yahoo Finance covering housing, mortgages, and home insurance.

item.title: Trump-backed housing rule could undercut effort to lower costs
item.author: Katy O'Donnell
item.description:
Trump-backed housing rule could undercut effort to lower costs
2026-10-13
Por Katy O'Donnell
https://finance.yahoo.com/real-estate/articles/trump-backed-housing-rule-could-104500803.html
(Bloomberg) -- A proposed rule change by the Trump administration could jeopardize billions of dollars of housing investment in rural areas and small towns – potentially undermining the White House's efforts to boost housing supply in order to bring down costs just as mortgage rates soar.
Most Read from Bloomberg
A 400-page rewrite of regulations under the Community Reinvestment Act – a landmark 1977 law requiring banks to invest in and provide services to local communities where they have a presence – would reclassify which financial institutions are subject to certain requirements, among other changes.
Comments on the proposal are due Oct. 13, but community development groups are pressing for an extension, and a Federal Reserve official recently detailed some of the agency's concerns. On Friday, a group of Democrats led by Senator Elizabeth Warren called for the immediate withdrawal of the proposal.
The critics warn that if carried out, the shift could leave more than 3.1 million additional people in a so-called "desert," a region with zero banks incentivized to provide community development financing, according to the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders.
"This administration has clearly stated that expanding affordable housing supply is a goal of theirs," said Sarah Brundage, president and chief executive officer of the NAAHL. "But the regulatory agenda is not aligning with that goal."
The CRA subjects banks to different tests based on the size of their assets. The new proposal, backed by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, would raise the "small" bank threshold to $1 billion in assets from $412 million and the "large" bank threshold to $10 billion from about $1.6 billion in assets. An intermediate tier of banks would have fewer requirements than large banks.
The expanded group of small banks would not be subject to rules about investments in community development, just retail lending. The new tier of intermediate-sized banks would have a community development test, but not an investment and service metric that large banks are graded on.
Opponents worry that the changes would mean less money getting invested in rural housing, precisely when housing affordability issues are hitting those areas the hardest.
Between 2000 and 2023, inflation-adjusted rents in rural areas increased by 31.2% while the median real income of rural renter households rose by just 5.5%, according to a report on "the deterioration of housing affordability in rural America" the White House released last year.
"The proposal would have a disproportionate impact on rural housing investments, and we think it would remove the strong incentive that currently exists for a number of banks to invest in affordable housing," said Emily Cadik, head of the Affordable Housing Tax Credit Coalition.
The White House contends that the new proposal would give banks more flexibility under the law and drive greater economic development. The new rules would not restrict banks' ability to count housing tax credit investments toward their CRA obligations, an administration official said.
When the Comptroller and the FDIC backed the proposed change in July, the Federal Reserve withheld its support. Fed Governor Michael Barr told attendees at a housing affordability conference last month that the regulator wants to avoid any "unintended consequences" with the proposed rule change.
"Community banks are really important all over the country, but especially in small towns and rural areas," Barr said. "So if you're not careful about how you look at the levels of tiering in a proposal, you might end up reducing the amount of capital going into affordable housing in rural areas and small towns, in particular, and
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: AMD launches Helion rack server for agentic AI
item.author: Daniel Howley
item.description:
AMD launches Helion rack server for agentic AI
2026-10-13
Por Daniel Howley
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/amd-launches-helion-rack-server-for-agentic-ai-132423849.html
AMD (AMD) is diving further into the agentic AI race with its new AMD Helion data center rack server.
Unveiled at the OCP Global Summit in San Jose, Calif., on Monday, Helion is designed to be outfitted with various configurations of CPUs and GPUs based on customers' needs.
The Helion is intended to serve as a reference design for AMD partners and clients, providing instructions for building the platforms.
The company said the server can be fully equipped with its sixth-generation EPYC CPUs for handling agentic AI tasks and servers, or configured with a collection of CPUs and its Instinct MI350P GPUs, which would serve as an all-purpose AI platform.
"Agentic AI is not one single workload. Agents are required for enterprise applications to running code and coordinating complex workflows," Dan McNamara, senior vice president and general manager of compute and enterprise AI at AMD, said in a statement.
"To do that takes optimized compute and infrastructure that can adapt to different workloads. With AMD Helion, we are bringing AMD EPYC performance, open software and flexible rack designs together so our partners can build systems around customer needs and make efficient use of available power," he added.
The move allows AMD to better compete with rival Nvidia (NVDA), which offers its own rack server reference designs, including its NVL72 servers.
AMD, like the rest of the chip industry, continues to benefit from the AI boom. The company topped analysts' estimates on the top and bottom lines during its most recent earnings report and provided a better-than-anticipated outlook for the current quarter.
Earnings per share rose 245%, while revenue climbed 50% to $11.5 billion.
Nvidia, however, continues to dominate in terms of sales, bringing in $96.2 billion in the prior quarter.
AMD stock, though, has outperformed Nvidia's over the last year, climbing roughly 182% year to date. Nvidia stock is up 25% in the same time period.
Read the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance

item.title: Broadcom CEO: Investors are ignoring a key lesson from Warren Buffett
item.author: Ethan Wolff-Mann
item.description:
Broadcom CEO: Investors are ignoring a key lesson from Warren Buffett
2026-10-13
Por Ethan Wolff-Mann
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/broadcom-ceo-investors-are-ignoring-a-key-lesson-from-warren-buffett-100000388.html
Warren Buffett famously advocated for investing in companies that you understand.
"What an investor needs is the ability to correctly evaluate selected businesses," he wrote in his 1996 letter to Berkshire Hathaway investors. "You only have to be able to evaluate companies within your circle of competence. The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital."
Broadcom (AVGO) CEO Hock Tan says too many people have blown past those boundaries and are blindly investing.
"A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in," he said in Singapore, Bloomberg reported. These investors, he added, have "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino."
Buffett himself was not always the most savvy tech investor, a fact he lamented when discussing Google, which was out of his "circle," so he bought very late. But the rise of even harder-to-understand AI stuff has made following this Buffett tenet way more difficult. We do not all have Ben Affleck-level AI comprehension (watch this if you haven't), and no one wants to get left behind.
It's easy to see where Tan and Buffett are coming from, and why the latter advocated for a simple index fund, arguing most people would be better off.
To be clear, Tan is bullish — he runs Broadcom. But in the long term, he's worried about the industry running out of capital and admits that profitability will hinge on proving AI's utility to businesses. Many of which, he said, might be just "wasting money."
Tan's reminder can be said another way: Yes, all the impressive AI things we see are very impressive. But they are also impressive in the same way a Ferrari is impressive — it can drive like that because it's expensive. And that it may not actually be that useful for its high cost in every business case.
Still, it's hard for regular retail investors not to see the massive bets made by Meta (META), Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL), and others and not assume they're simply following an entity that knows more than they do about the technology and its implications — with conviction strong enough to bet huge on it.

item.content:encoded:
Broadcom CEO: Investors are ignoring a key lesson from Warren Buffett

2026-10-13

Por Ethan Wolff-Mann

https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/broadcom-ceo-investors-are-ignoring-a-key-lesson-from-warren-buffett-100000388.html

Warren Buffett famously advocated for investing in companies that you understand.

"What an investor needs is the ability to correctly evaluate selected businesses," he wrote in his 1996 letter to Berkshire Hathaway investors. "You only have to be able to evaluate companies within your circle of competence. The size of that circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries, however, is vital."

Broadcom (AVGO) CEO Hock Tan says too many people have blown past those boundaries and are blindly investing.

"A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in," he said in Singapore, Bloomberg reported. These investors, he added, have "extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino."

Buffett himself was not always the most savvy tech investor, a fact he lamented when discussing Google, which was out of his "circle," so he bought very late. But the rise of even harder-to-understand AI stuff has made following this Buffett tenet way more difficult. We do not all have Ben Affleck-level AI comprehension (watch this if you haven't), and no one wants to get left behind.

It's easy to see where Tan and Buffett are coming from, and why the latter advocated for a simple index fund, arguing most people would be better off.

To be clear, Tan is bullish — he runs Broadcom. But in the long term, he's worried about the industry running out of capital and admits that profitability will hinge on proving AI's utility to businesses. Many of which, he said, might be just "wasting money."

Tan's reminder can be said another way: Yes, all the impressive AI things we see are very impressive. But they are also impressive in the same way a Ferrari is impressive — it can drive like that because it's expensive. And that it may not actually be that useful for its high cost in every business case.

Still, it's hard for regular retail investors not to see the massive bets made by Meta (META), Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL), and others and not assume they're simply following an entity that knows more than they do about the technology and its implications — with conviction strong enough to bet huge on it.

But perhaps the lesson is in the nuance of Tan's comments: Avoid the "casino" aspect of the AI trade, not necessarily the trade itself. With a huge chunk of the S&P 500 bolstered by AI, you can't anyway, even if you heed the Oracle of Omaha's still-relevant advice.

item.title: Businesses Risk Wave of Democratic Probes on Costs, Corruption
item.author: Caitlin Reilly
item.description:
Businesses Risk Wave of Democratic Probes on Costs, Corruption
2026-10-13
Por Caitlin Reilly
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/businesses-risk-wave-democratic-probes-110000821.html
(Bloomberg) -- Private businesses risk an onslaught of congressional investigations if Democrats prevail in midterm elections as the opposition party prepares to concentrate sweeping oversight powers on allegations of Trump administration corruption and public anger over the cost of living.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Companies including Amazon.com Inc. and Nvidia Corp. have already been hit with investigative inquiries from Democrats who could compel testimony if the party secures a congressional majority.
"There's a cost to the American people of the out-of-control corruption that has been visited upon them by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists," House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries declared last month, as lawmakers left Washington for full-time campaigning. "We're going to hold the crooks accountable beginning on Day One."
Trump retains a veto over legislation for two more years, regardless of the election results. Not so over a new majority's oversight authority, which it can wield as a potent political weapon through attention-grabbing public hearings and damaging investigative revelations.
On consumer issues, key Democrats likely to gain subpoena power are showing continued interest in scrutinizing the party's perennial corporate punching bags in healthcare, tech, housing and financial services, as well as new targets related to surveillance pricing, data centers and artificial intelligence.
Companies and corporate executives also would be in the crosshairs of Democratic probes of Trump administration ethics controversies. Businesses perceived to have profited from ties to the White House would be targets — and with fewer legal privileges than the executive branch offer the quickest route to revelations that could ignite public outcry.
Amazon.com Inc., Apple Inc., Comcast Corp., Meta Platforms Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Nvidia Corp. have already been hit with letters from Democratic lawmakers demanding information on donations to Trump's ballroom. Such letters typically telegraph investigative objectives.
Plenty of companies aren't waiting for the election to get ready.
"Many corporate clients, in particular, are acutely aware that there is a dark cloud looming on the horizon just past the beginning of November, and that there is going to be a broad wave of congressional investigations directed against Corporate America," said Robert Kelner, who leads Covington & Burling's congressional investigations practice.
Congressional probes can exact a heavy toll. Tobacco executives faced lengthy perjury investigations following testimony in a 1994 hearing on nicotine and addiction. Wells Fargo & Co.'s then-chief executive officer, John Stumpf, resigned and forfeited millions in compensation weeks after two bruising back-to-back 2016 hearings on the bank's creation of fake accounts. Three Ivy League university presidents quit under pressure following a 2023 hearing on student protests over Gaza.
Trump Ties
Democrats have made clear Trump and the administration's alleged corruption will be center stage next year. With cooperation from the executive branch unlikely, lawmakers are likely to quickly turn their attention to private-sector entities in Trump's orbit, former congressional investigators said.
The private sector lacks legal privileges the executive branch can use to slow walk congressional investigations. They also risk alienating customers and shareholders if they openly defy Congress.
The corporate world's courting of the administration through donations to the president's pet projects, as well as the deals cut with the administration to offer equity stakes, lower drug prices and tariff exemptions offer Democrats a rich target environment.
Companies are likely to receive an "awful lot of subpoenas and demands in
[Transcripcion recortada]

item.title: Great results won't be good enough for this AI earnings season
item.author: Hamza Shaban
item.description:
Great results won't be good enough for this AI earnings season
2026-10-13
Por Hamza Shaban
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/great-results-wont-be-good-enough-for-this-ai-earnings-season-100000670.html
The stock market is an expectations game. But when they keep rising, the goalposts can move so far that even powerful tech earnings can trigger a sell-off.
This is a key risk to consider as we head into another earnings season, where AI spending and returns on investment will be top of mind and a key takeaway will be how much further companies have to extend their beats to even move the needle.
After two quarters of big, positive surprises — and index gains to show for it — healthy earnings beats have become the status quo, according to Bank of America strategist Savita Subramanian, in a note on Monday. What investors are really looking for is whether the growth can be sustained in 2027.
"Ultimately, index [earnings per share] remains highly dependent on the durability of the AI capex cycle and successful monetization," she wrote.
That's a theme investors have seen before.
No doubt, Big Tech management will spend their energy and earnings calls emphasizing how their massive build-out spending is tied to insatiable demand. Analysts expect sustained strength in AI-related investment. As Bank of America notes, the top five hyperscalers are on pace to grow capex by more than 110% year over year in Q3.
But as we've seen in mixed results among names like Meta (META), Google (GOOG), Amazon (AMZN), and Microsoft (MSFT), a lot will depend on executives convincing analysts and investors that monetization is already being realized or is just around the corner. Spending, and the willingness to risk it, isn't in itself enough of a positive signal for Wall Street.
As Subramanian wrote, Q3 beats are expected, but further upside likely depends on confidence that strong growth can extend into 2027.
This season is especially challenging because while the AI spending impulse is in play, the economic environment is changing around it. Rates are higher and are expected to rise again, coupled with significant commodity pressure. Next year, there's more room for things to go wrong. (Not to mention the political uncertainty heading into the November elections.)
"The interplay between geopolitics, rates and Tech may be underestimated — a higher cost of capital and geopolitical bottlenecks could gum up what has so far been a mostly smooth story," Subramanian wrote.
Much will depend on the ability of Big Tech companies to pull off what might be described as an immaculate quarter. They've done it before. Exceptional beats have become all too common. But the bar keeps rising along the external risks that aren't strictly within their control. This time it's not just hitting the marks on spending and the revenue projections, but communicating with confidence that the astounding growth will continue.
Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Follow Hamza on X @hshaban.

item.title: Microsoft reveals Maia 300 AI chip as it works to reduce dependence on Nvidia, AMD
item.author: Daniel Howley
item.description:
Microsoft reveals Maia 300 AI chip as it works to reduce dependence on Nvidia, AMD
2026-10-13
Por Daniel Howley
https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/article/microsoft-reveals-maia-300-ai-chip-as-it-works-to-reduce-dependence-on-nvidia-amd-130000212.html
Microsoft (MSFT) has debuted its latest AI chip, the Azure Maia 300, as it looks to reduce its reliance on third-party processors from the likes of Nvidia (NVDA) and AMD (AMD).
Unveiled at the OCP Global Summit 2026 in San Jose on Monday, the Maia 300 will join Microsoft's Maia 200 and Maia 100 chips as part of what the company said will be multigigawatt deployments beginning next year.
The Windows maker said that will make its Maia chips the "primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services."
The company said Maia 300 provides 40% more tokens per megawatt than "leading GPU-based systems," a clear swipe at Nvidia, and that a 96-chip rack offers seven times the rack-scale token throughput of Microsoft's Maia 200.
Tokens are a basic unit of measurement in AI systems that can represent parts of words, images, and videos.
The more tokens per megawatt, the more efficient an AI rack.
The Maia 200 chip currently powers its Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, as well as OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) models, Microsoft's MAI models, and open-source models. That provides 1.7 times more tokens per watt for AI capabilities in Microsoft's Teams, Copilot, and Cowork software versus other GPU-based systems, the company said.
Microsoft and fellow hyperscaler peers Amazon (AMZN), Google (GOOG, GOOGL), and Meta (META), as well as AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic (ANTH.PVT), either already offer or are working on their own custom chips.
Doing so acts as a hedge against becoming overdependent on processors from Nvidia and AMD. Producing their own semiconductors also allows companies to tailor them to their specific needs.
That's a potential problem for Nvidia, which regularly generates upwards of 50% of its quarterly revenue from hyperscalers.
On top of that, Amazon and Google now rent out their custom chips to third-party customers, a direct threat to Nvidia's business. What's more, Amazon is looking into selling chips for customers to install in their own data centers rather than running them from Amazon's own facilities.
That doesn't necessarily mean hyperscalers will stop purchasing Nvidia chips entirely. Customers still want access to a number of chips for different workloads, meaning the Amazons and Microsofts of the world will need to continue stocking up on the most in-demand processors.
And for now, those are Nvidia's.

That provides 1.7 times more tokens per watt for AI capabilities in Microsoft's Teams, Copilot, and Cowork software versus other GPU-based systems, the company said.
Microsoft and fellow hyperscaler peers Amazon (AMZN), Google (GOOG, GOOGL), and Meta (META), as well as AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic (ANTH.PVT), either already offer or are working on their own custom chips.
Doing so acts as a hedge against becoming overdependent on processors from Nvidia and AMD. Producing their own semiconductors also allows companies to tailor them to their specific needs.
That's a potential problem for Nvidia, which regularly generates upwards of 50% of its quarterly revenue from hyperscalers.
On top of that, Amazon and Google now rent out their custom chips to third-party customers, a direct threat to Nvidia's business. What's more, Amazon is looking into selling chips for customers to install in their own data centers rather than running them from Amazon's own facilities.
That doesn't necessarily mean hyperscalers will stop purchasing Nvidia chips entirely. Customers still want access to a number of chips for different workloads, meaning the Amazons and Microsofts of the world will need to continue stocking up on the most in-demand processors.
And for now, those are Nvidia's.

item.title: Why bank stocks shocked everyone by getting thrashed
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
Why bank stocks shocked everyone by getting thrashed
2026-10-13
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/why-bank-stocks-shocked-everyone-by-getting-thrashed-141552354.html
So much for bank stocks loving higher interest rates.
That old saw is being completely ignored ahead of earnings from big banks, which kick off this week with numbers out of JPMorgan (JPM), Bank of America (BAC), Goldman Sachs (GS), and Wells Fargo (WFC).
Share prices across the entire banking sector have flat-out crashed, placing many top names in correction territory — down 10% from their highs.
Over the past month, JPMorgan has shed 6%, Citigroup is down 6.5%, Wells Fargo is off 7%, Morgan Stanley (MS) is down 11%, Goldman Sachs is down 12%, and Bank of America is down 13%.
Even the KBW Nasdaq Bank Index (^BKX), which tracks the 24 publicly traded US banking stocks, is now down more than 14% from its August peak.
"This means if the Bank Index continues to drop even with the S&P 500 hitting new highs, it could be a major warning sign for the US stock market," the team at the Macro Paper said.
Read more: Wall Street banks had a blockbuster first half. Higher rates will test the boom.
Pros point to a few factors for the surprise sell-off despite the US economy continuing to chug along.
The first is what may be a less lucrative market for deals in the near term amid concerns about sky-high valuations on tech companies. To that end, it's unlikely OpenAI's (OPAI.PVT) IPO will happen this year, and others thought to be coming to market are on pause.
"Indeed Oura's delayed IPO while the generational OpenAI offering expected this year being pushed back to 2027 has raised fears of a deteriorating funding environment. Deposit competition from AI offerings maximizing cash yields has also weighed on sentiment," Evercore ISI strategist Julian Emanuel said.
The other issue at play is the perception that new technology will meaningfully disrupt the financial services space in the years to come. For example, companies such as Robinhood (HOOD) and Coinbase (COIN) have unveiled new agentic trading capabilities for their customers. (Disclosure: Yahoo Finance has a partnership with Coinbase.)
Emanuel explained, "Focus this reporting season will first be placed intently on Financials, whose recent underperformance has been striking. The sector has historically been a beneficiary of higher interest rates (supporting net interest margins) but has fallen precipitously since yields have spiked above 5% and as some perceive a threat to financials' margins with the debut of consumer AI Agent Muse."

item.title: A handful of tech stocks are masking an ugly S&P 500 problem
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
A handful of tech stocks are masking an ugly S&P 500 problem
2026-10-13
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/a-handful-of-tech-stocks-are-masking-an-ugly-sp-500-problem-133611321.html
Thank goodness for the likes of Nvidia (NVDA), Micron (MU), and a few other high-profile tech stocks in the S&P 500 (^GSPC).
Without their strong gains, the S&P 500 would be looking ugly — and far from hovering at record highs.
About 84% of S&P 500 stocks are now trading at least 10% below their all-time highs, according to new analysis from the Kobeissi Letter.
The Real Estate (XLRE) sector leads the pullback, with 97% of its stocks down at least 10%, followed by Materials (XLB) at 96%, Utilities (XLU) at 94%, and Consumer Discretionary (XLY) at 92%.
Pressure in these spaces likely reflects concerns about earnings from companies exposed to high interest rates, notably in housing and retail.
Energy, meanwhile, has held up relatively better, with 62% of stocks in the sector more than 10% below their all-time highs, followed by Healthcare (XLV) at 70% and Technology (XLK) at 72%.
What's more, 59% of S&P 500 stocks are down at least 20% from their highs, 41% are down more than 30%, and 17% are off by more than 50%.
"A few names are carrying the entire stock market," strategists at the Kobeissi Letter rightly pointed out.
Read more: How to protect your money during turmoil, stock market volatility
Yet despite the drawdowns underneath the surface of the S&P 500, the market is celebrating a milestone.
Investors are currently living in the 11th bull market since the 1950s, which is on track to become the seventh to complete at least four full years on Oct. 12, per data from Truist co-chief investment officer Keith Lerner.
Measured against every bull market dating back to the 1950s, the 119% advance sits near the middle of the pack, well below the 401% gain during the 2009 to 2020 cycle and the 582% gain from 1987 to 2000.
The historical average advance for a bull market in Lerner's measurement period is 184%. Of the 10 prior bull markets, six lasted longer than four years.

item.title: She Was Offered 40 Million for Silence on Elon Musk
item.author: Texto propio
item.description:
She Was Offered 40 Million for Silence on Elon Musk
2026-10-12
Por Texto propio
She Was Offered $40 Million for Silence on Elon Musk. She Spoke Out Instead.
By Coralie Kraft
October 9, 2026
Ashley St. Clair is sick of people asking her the same questions about Elon Musk. “People treat me like I’m some Elon psychoanalyst,” she said during a visit to The New York Times in September. “They want to know, ‘What’s it like to hang out with him?’ or they say, ‘Not many people have spent time with him one-on-one.’” She sighed. “It’s annoying and laborious.”
You can’t blame them for asking. St. Clair, a former conservative influencer, gave birth to one of Musk’s children in 2024. (At the time, she also had another child from a previous relationship.) This fall, she’s a significant figure in “Musk,” Alex Gibney’s nearly four-hour-long documentary about the world’s first trillionaire, and she has more pressing points. “This is about a deeper rot in our society, where we’ve equated capital with morality,” she said. “There’s a level of societal and individual trust that we give to people if they have money.”
Musk did not respond to requests for comment. After TMZ reported that Ashley St. Clair rejected a $40 million N.D.A., Musk responded via X, stating, “She was never offered that and has a history of making false claims.” He also condemned Gibney’s documentary with another post on X reading, “Gibney just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don’t even know me.”
Gibney, the Oscar-winning documentary filmmaker, first met St. Clair in December 2025. “Beyond Musk’s baby obsession, Ashley had a front-row seat during the 2024 campaign and was able to tell me things I didn’t know about Musk’s motivations,” he said in an email. Below, St. Clair shares her side of the story.
These are edited excerpts from the conversation.
Were you at all nervous about participating in the film?
No. I was familiar with some of Alex’s documentary work, like “Going Clear.” I liked that he didn’t have any fear. He has a history of treating facts and narratives with respect.
You’ve seen the film. How did you feel watching it?
What was both validating and terrifying was the way the narratives harmonized. Me, Justine [Wilson, Musk’s first wife], Sam Harris [the New Atheist philosopher] and Geoffrey Hinton [the so-called Godfather of A.I.] — there are so many similarities in our experiences with Elon. I think when you’re able to take people who have never spoken to each other and harmonize a narrative, that is the truth.
A woman with long dark hair wearing a brown sleeveless top looks toward the camera.
“I would say it felt emotionally intimate. We were in contact every day,” St. Clair said about her relationship with Musk. Credit... Elinor Kry for The New York Times
What did your life look like when you met Musk in 2023?
How did you feel when he followed you?
I don’t think people understand the number of eyeballs that were on everyone Elon interacted with at that time. I was getting “Congratulations!” texts from people in MAGA. Right away, there were people saying, “She’s going to be his next baby mama.” I was about to turn 24.
And when did you meet in person for the first time?
Did it feel like a romantic relationship?
I would say it felt emotionally intimate. We were in contact every day. But also I was never like, “I’m the chosen one.” At the time, he was this savior of free speech, and I was very wrapped up in all of that. I’d say there was a bit of idolization going on, too.
When did you start talking about having a child together?
In January 2024, we went on vacation to St. Bart’s, and he said, “You should have 10 kids! Let’s have a kid. My only limited resource is time.”
What did that mean to you?
I wanted more children, so it meant that I would always be able to take care of my kids financially. Also, within MAGA, it was seen as a stain on your character to be a single mom. So to have this bastion of the rig
[Transcripcion recortada]

What did that mean to you?

item.title: DOJ Urges Companies to Self Disclose Fraud and Avoid Prosecution
item.author: Jimmy Jenkins
item.description:
DOJ Urges Companies to Self Disclose Fraud and Avoid Prosecution
2026-10-12
Por Jimmy Jenkins
https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/doj-urges-companies-self-disclose-165231597.html
(Bloomberg) -- The head of the US Justice Department's Criminal Division is urging companies to self report possible fraud, favoring settlements with companies that proactively disclose potential violations over what could become costly and time-consuming prosecutions.
Most Read from Bloomberg
The approach has prompted criticism from some public-interest groups that President Donald Trump's second administration is being soft on crime, with one group publishing a report Wednesday listing the "cancellation" of more than 200 enforcement actions inherited from the Biden administration. Those actions include ending federal investigations, lawsuits, and settlements.
Assistant Attorney General Tysen Duva said in an interview with Bloomberg News that the approach is already paying off for the Justice Department. In the coming months, he said he will be announcing corporate enforcement policy resolutions, non-prosecution agreements and deferred-prosecution agreements with companies, and charges against individuals that were a result of self disclosures.
"It is better to try to obtain cooperation from an entity and provide incentives for them to come in and tell you what happened," Duva said. "Because if they don't, it's up to a whistleblower or a confidential informant. And then you get in this lengthy, protracted litigation."
Duva said if the Justice Department is able to convince companies to come in early and self disclose, his agency can truncate — and in some cases eliminate — a costly legal process. He said his emphasis on self-disclosure followed a precedent set before he was tapped to run the Criminal Division last year.
Duva was elevated from his previous post as a Jacksonville, Florida-based assistant US attorney in July of 2025, and confirmed by the Senate the following December.
"We really want to try to allay some fears and communicate very clearly that this means if you come in, and you self disclose, that you can obtain the declination, but you have to fully cooperate," Duva said. "It is laying out what you learned, how you learned it, and who did it. And as part of that, you would take that information and pursue charges against individuals."
The Justice Department pointed to a resolution reached in March with medical device company Balt SAS as an example a self-disclosure success. The department said the company disclosed and took steps to remediate the behavior. In return, DOJ declined to prosecute Balt as a company, instead bringing charges against two individuals. The company also agreed to pay $1.2 million in disgorgement.

DOJ Urges Companies to Self Disclose Fraud and Avoid Prosecution

2026-10-12

Por Jimmy Jenkins

https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/doj-urges-companies-self-disclose-165231597.html

(Bloomberg) -- The head of the US Justice Department's Criminal Division is urging companies to self report possible fraud, favoring settlements with companies that proactively disclose potential violations over what could become costly and time-consuming prosecutions.

Most Read from Bloomberg

The approach has prompted criticism from some public-interest groups that President Donald Trump's second administration is being soft on crime, with one group publishing a report Wednesday listing the "cancellation" of more than 200 enforcement actions inherited from the Biden administration. Those actions include ending federal investigations, lawsuits, and settlements.

Assistant Attorney General Tysen Duva said in an interview with Bloomberg News that the approach is already paying off for the Justice Department. In the coming months, he said he will be announcing corporate enforcement policy resolutions, non-prosecution agreements and deferred-prosecution agreements with companies, and charges against individuals that were a result of self disclosures.

"It is better to try to obtain cooperation from an entity and provide incentives for them to come in and tell you what happened," Duva said. "Because if they don't, it's up to a whistleblower or a confidential informant. And then you get in this lengthy, protracted litigation."

Duva said if the Justice Department is able to convince companies to come in early and self disclose, his agency can truncate — and in some cases eliminate — a costly legal process. He said his emphasis on self-disclosure followed a precedent set before he was tapped to run the Criminal Division last year.

Duva was elevated from his previous post as a Jacksonville, Florida-based assistant US attorney in July of 2025, and confirmed by the Senate the following December.

"We really want to try to allay some fears and communicate very clearly that this means if you come in, and you self disclose, that you can obtain the declination, but you have to fully cooperate," Duva said. "It is laying out what you learned, how you learned it, and who did it. And as part of that, you would take that information and pursue charges against individuals."

The Justice Department pointed to a resolution reached in March with medical device company Balt SAS as an example a self-disclosure success. The department said the company disclosed and took steps to remediate the behavior. In return, DOJ declined to prosecute Balt as a company, instead bringing charges against two individuals. The company also agreed to pay $1.2 million in disgorgement.

item.title: The AI SaaSpocalypse was supposed to crush software stocks — but this happened instead
item.author: Brian Sozzi
item.description:
The AI SaaSpocalypse was supposed to crush software stocks — but this happened instead
2026-10-12
Por Brian Sozzi
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/the-ai-saaspocalypse-was-supposed-to-crush-software-stocks--but-this-happened-instead-163021702.html
So much for the SaaSpocalypse eating all software stocks alive until they hit $0.
The overused 2026 market slang — which promoted the view that AI players like Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) and OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) would crush the business models of software-as-a-service companies — should be put to bed. Because after a stretch where this narrative hammered many software players, most have rallied sharply back.
And with good reason.
The broader software group and the IGV index have rallied significantly since the end of June, JPMorgan strategist Samik Chatterjee pointed out (see the chart below), up 21% since the end of the month relative to the broader S&P 500 (^GSPC), up 4%. Some of the top performers include Paycom (PAYC), DocuSign (DOCU), Workday (WDAY), Salesforce (CRM), Cloudflare (NET), Twilio (TWLO), and Microsoft (MSFT).
The broader rally has, in part, been helped by a valuation multiple rerating across infrastructure and application software companies, Chatterjee noted.
Renewed belief in software stocks could be sustained into year-end as investors digest third quarter earnings reports.
"Heading into C3Q earnings, we expect the broader share price momentum for the group to continue with infrastructure software companies leading the way on account of the AI-led tailwinds driving robust beats on both top-line and earnings, albeit potentially only in line on gross margins," Chatterjee said.
He added, "We expect application software companies to also participate in the positive share price momentum for the sector into the year-end on account of raises to full-year guides, aided by building momentum in AI monetization, which is steadily building as incremental revenue on top of the core businesses, which range from modestly decelerating to stable growth across our coverage companies."

item.title: For the first time ever, 10-year bond yields track diesel prices more closely than crude, and Trump’s fuel deal with Putin may be too little too late
item.author: Jason Ma
item.description:
For the first time ever, 10-year bond yields track diesel prices more closely than crude, and Trump’s fuel deal with Putin may be too little too late
2026-10-12
Por Jason Ma
https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/first-time-ever-10-bond-171218177.html
For the first time ever, 10-year bond yields track diesel prices more closely than crude, and Trump’s fuel deal with Putin may be too little too late
Diesel prices have come off their all-time highs in recent weeks, but the key industrial fuel has already moved the needle across the economy and financial markets, making affordability a more potent issue in the midterm elections.
The national average for diesel is about $6.277 per gallon, according to AAA, down from its $6.528 high but still 71% above year-ago levels. By contrast, U.S. crude oil is up 56% from a year earlier as damage to refining capacity in the Middle East and Russia has produced a sharper crunch in fuel markets.
Because diesel is a critical input in manufacturing, agriculture and logistics, the recent price surge has been felt broadly. The latest consumer and producer price indexes showed jumps in transportation costs, while purchasing manager surveys signaled big spikes in prices businesses are paying.
"This is why products have been trading at double the price of crude during the past few months, something that has never happened before. Ultimately, diesel and gasoline drive inflation, not crude oil," Amrita Sen, director of market intelligence and co-founder at Energy Aspects, wrote in the Financial Times on Wednesday.
And as higher fuel costs keep inflation forecasts elevated, markets are pricing in a more hawkish Federal Reserve that's ready to hike rates further. Bond yields have risen in anticipation of tighter monetary policy, raising borrowing costs for consumers.
Crude prices had previously moved in tandem with prices for refined products and had long been a proxy for those costs, but that relationship has broken down, according to Sen.
"In fact, since May, 10-year US Treasury yields have correlated more closely with diesel prices than crude prices, for the first time ever," she added.
That's why the Trump administration has started paying more attention lately to bringing down diesel prices, Sen said.
Over the past week alone, President Donald Trump has taken steps to ease the cost burden. On Monday, he signed an executive order to defer the 24-cent federal tax per gallon on diesel until the end of the year, though most states have separate levies on diesel.
And on Friday, he said he reached a deal with Vladimir Putin to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal from years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine.
Russia will supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel now, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter," according to Trump. Russia will deliver another 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that.

item.title: Bond yields are surging worldwide — and France is on the 'ugly side': Chart of the Day
item.author: Ines Ferré
item.description:
Bond yields are surging worldwide — and France is on the 'ugly side': Chart of the Day
2026-10-12
Por Ines Ferré
https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/bond-yields-are-surging-worldwide--and-france-is-on-the-ugly-side-chart-of-the-day-123643553.html
It's not just the US seeing a rapid rise in bond yields. The surge in Treasury yields worldwide is raising alarm bells among investors.
"Any lingering doubts about whether the world has truly left the era of low interest rates behind should now be quashed," Thomas Garretson, senior portfolio strategist at RBC Wealth Management, wrote in a recent note.
Longer-dated bond yields have been flagging issues "that have been percolating in global bond markets for years, which are now coming to a head," he noted.
Wall Street strategists see an array of reasons behind the rise in yields.
"On the good side of the spectrum, better-than-expected economic growth has driven US bond yields up to levels that are back to normal," Ed Yardeni of Yardeni Research wrote last week.
"On the ugly side, soaring bond yields in France are signaling a looming debt crisis," he said.
The protests over public education funding across major French cities have coincided with surging bond yields.
Macquarie strategists have argued that there is a "direct and self-reinforcing causal connection" between recent street riots over proposed budget cuts in France and the country's bond market stress.
Behind France, the US 10-year yield (^TNX) has posted its biggest jump among more than 20 countries tracked by Yardeni Research.
Italy, Indonesia, Japan, and South Korea have also seen their benchmark yields rise at least 100 basis points since the start of the year.
Rising yields are also attributed to higher oil prices stemming from the war in the Middle East and the unwinding of the yen-carry trade.
Japanese investors, who accumulated over $1.3 trillion in US Treasurys during the era of negative domestic rates, have been repatriating capital as domestic yields normalize.
RBC research estimates that every $100 billion shift in Japanese holdings impacts 10-year Treasury yields by roughly 50 basis points. As of July 2026, Japan's holdings are down $120 billion so far this year and about $300 billion from their 2021 peak.
As the US 10-year Treasury yield hangs near its highest level in 24 years, strategists are seeing a risk of 6% for the first time since 2000.
Even as bond yields revert to their levels prior to the 2008 financial crisis, strong earnings reports, coupled with a pause in interest rate hikes from the Fed, are expected to keep the stock market rally intact headed into the end of the year.
Seasonal tailwinds during midterm election years also favor a positive return for the S&P 500 this quarter.
Ines Ferre is a Senior Business Reporter for Yahoo Finance covering the US stock market, publicly traded companies, and commodities.

item.title: Zelenskyy Risks Rupture With Trump as Midterms Pressure Mounts
item.author: Aliaksandr Kudrytski; Natalia Drozdiak; Alberto Nardelli
item.description:
Zelenskyy Risks Rupture With Trump as Midterms Pressure Mounts
2026-10-12
Por Aliaksandr Kudrytski; Natalia Drozdiak; Alberto Nardelli
https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/zelenskyy-risks-rupture-trump-midterms-020024586.html
(Bloomberg) -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is on a collision course with President Donald Trump, who is increasingly looking at Kyiv's battle against Russia primarily through the lens of energy prices ahead of US midterm elections.
Most Read from Bloomberg
Trump sprung an announcement of an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine on Zelenskyy, as the US leader pushes for him to stop bombing Russian oil refineries and defends a controversial deal with Vladimir Putin on diesel exports.
After Trump posted on social media about the ceasefire, Zelenskyy said he is willing to accept it, but only if Russia does too — his long-standing position — making clear his significant doubts about that prospect.
"Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well," Zelenskyy said on social media, adding that he is "awaiting details" from the US on the deal.
But as Ukraine continues to respond to Russia's invasion with its own attacks on refineries, Zelenskyy increasingly risks running afoul of Trump. That poses a hazard for Kyiv as it still relies on US weapon purchases that are financed by other NATO allies and on intelligence-sharing from Washington. Ukraine is also strapped for cash ahead of the fifth winter of the war.
A day before his ceasefire announcement — the second in as many months — Trump lashed out at Zelenskyy, suggesting he should consider stepping aside as Ukraine's president. On Friday, after Trump reached the diesel export deal with Putin, Ukrainian negotiators cut short their talks in Miami with US envoys, according to people familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
In the meeting, US negotiators, led by Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, told Ukrainian officials that the US was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence, and so Ukraine shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers like striking refineries, according to one of the people. That was perceived as an implied threat from the US to cut off intelligence to Kyiv, several of the people said. The Financial Times was first to report about the intelligence cutoff remark at the Miami meeting.
European officials present at the meeting received no prior notification from the US on the imminent diesel deal with Moscow, one person said.
Ahead of US midterms in November, the Trump administration is scrambling to bring down soaring fuel prices, which have raised costs for farmers and truckers. But the deal with Russia, which would release Russian diesel to global markets, risks sparking geopolitical backlash without boosting supply enough to materially lower prices.
It's also triggered significant bipartisan pushback in the US. Seven US senators — four Republicans and three Democrats — released a statement pointing out that Congress had banned imports of Russian energy since 2022, and that the deal was illegal.
After years of devastating Russian aerial barrages, Ukraine has developed an increasingly effective strategy of hitting sensitive parts of the Kremlin's economy with long-range drones in an effort to undermine Putin's ability to finance the war.
The attacks forced the Kremlin to pay oil companies steep subsidies to supply road fuels to the domestic market and ban diesel exports, which now also raises questions about Moscow's ability to fulfill its deal with Trump. On Saturday, Russia partially lifted its ban on diesel exports, allowing 500,000 metric tons of fuel to reach international markets.
Tensions between the US president and Zelenskyy have come and gone since Trump returned to the White House with a pledge to quickly end the war in Ukraine. Last year,

Zelenskyy Risks Rupture With Trump as Midterms Pressure Mounts

Por Aliaksandr Kudrytski; Natalia Drozdiak; Alberto Nardelli
